newsitem.title: USA: Annan says accord on Cyprus "within our grasp".
newsitem.headline: Annan says accord on Cyprus "within our grasp".

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said on Wednesday that an end to the division of Cyprus was within reach but the consequences of failure could be more dire than at any time in recent decades.

He was opening five days of U.N.-sponsored talks between the leaders of the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities, President Glafcos Clerides and Rauf Denktash, aimed at reviving negotiations on establishing a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.
"I invited the leaders of the Cypriot communities to meet here for face-to-face talks because I believe that a lasting peace in Cyprus is now within our grasp," Annan said at an opening ceremony.

The talks are being held at a picturesque resort called Troutbeck, 90 miles (145 km) north of New York city. It is a more luxurious setting than the airbase at Dayton, Ohio, where the U.S.-sponsored 1995 Bosnia peace talks were held. But the United Nations still seeks seclusion to prevent the two leaders -- long-time diplomatic sparring partners -- from jabbing at each other through the media.

Clerides and Denktash met for the first time in nearly three years at a dinner the U.N. chief gave at his residence Tuesday night. Wearing dark business suits, they sat on either side of Annan at Wednesday's ceremonial opening and later posed for handshakes and chatted amicably.
Annan said his special envoy for Cyprus who will chair the talks, former Ecuadorean Foreign Minister Diego Cordovez, would submit "a number of suggestions" to facilitate the work.

"If you agree with these suggestions, you will be sending a strong and unmistakable signal to the international community. You will be signalling your commitment and determination to reach a comprehensive settlement -- for which the people of Cyprus have been waiting for too long," he said.

Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since troops from Turkey took over the north of the island in 1974 in reaction to a coup in Nicosia backed by the junta then ruling Greece. The Turkish Cypriots proclaimed their own state in 1983 with Denktash as president but it is recognised only by Ankara.

The Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain, when a government representing both communities broke apart amid violence that resulted in the dispatch of a U.N. peacekeeping force that is still on the island.
In his speech, Annan said young Cypriots were growing up under a "cloud of uncertainty and potential instability".
"For their sake, this cannot continue. There is a sense of greater urgency, more of a consensus than ever that this dispute must be brought to an end," he said.

"The consequences of failure are likely to be more dire than at any time in recent decades," he added, apparently alluding to forthcoming events that could precipitate a crisis embroiling historic antagonists Greece and Turkey.
These include talks expected to begin next year on European Union membership for Cyprus and the Nicosia government's planned deployment of Russian-made S-300 air defence missiles.

Turkey and the Turkish Cypriots, who do not recognise the Greek Cypriot-led government, say it cannot negotiate EU membership for the entire island. Any move in that direction would result in linking northern Cyprus even more closely with Turkey, they say.
Turkey, with air bases little more than 40 miles (65 km) from Cyprus, has also said it would take any steps necessary to prevent the deployment next year of the S-300 missiles.
Some 30,000 Turkish soldiers are still in northern Cyprus while the Nicosia government, which has a defence pact with Greece, has been acquiring advanced weapons.
Annan said the Cypriot communities would earn international respect and gratitude if they reached agreement.

The world would also be profoundly relieved "at the removal of a potential flashpoint from international relations in the Eastern Mediterranean." Most importantly, an accord would "provide a prosperous and peaceful future for all Cypriots."
Annan noted that the first Cyprus inter-communal talks were held 29 years ago -- led by Clerides and Denktash as presidents of their respective communal parliaments.
Efforts involving four previous U.N. secretaries-general had provided an approach for tackling crucial issues, he said.
